title: What Makes Lead So Poisonous?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain lead as an element and why it is toxic. They cover the Flint, Michigan water crisis and how Flint's corrosive river water leached lead from old pipes. They trace lead's history from Roman plumbing and the plumbum etymology to lead paint, leaded gasoline and knocking, and tetraethyl lead's phase-out. They describe lead sources today (batteries, electronics, leaded glass, old houses), how lead is mined and smelted from galena, and its biological effects, since the body mistakes lead for calcium and it harms neurons, brain development and nearly every organ system. They discuss blood testing, chelation therapy, the controversial lead-crime hypothesis from Kevin Drum's Mother Jones article, and the Flint lawsuits and sovereign immunity issues. The episode ends with a listener letter from an American living in Finland about low corruption and high taxes.

segments.title: Opening banter and sponsor read
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about frozen burritos and a Squarespace sponsor read, then introduce the episode on lead and the Flint, Michigan water scandal.

segments.title: Flint water crisis background
segments.summary: Overview of Flint's switch from Detroit water to the Flint River, the corrosive water, Buick City pollution, hair loss and rashes, and the state's denials and residents' citizen-science push.

segments.title: History of lead and lead pipes
segments.summary: Lead pipes used since Roman times, the etymology of plumbing from plumbum and the symbol Pb, and lead's properties such as malleability, corrosion resistance and poor conductivity that make it useful in pipes and solder.

segments.title: Lead paint, packaging ink and toys
segments.summary: Lead in paint and signage, lead ink on bread bags, the 2007 Chinese product recalls including Dora the Explorer and Sesame Street toys, and the 1978 US lead paint ban. Brief digression about the band Urban Dance Squad.

segments.title: Leaded glass, Baltimore ban and leaded gasoline
segments.summary: Leaded glass and its uses, Baltimore's early lead paint ban and federal Lead Poisoning Prevention Act, and tetraethyl lead added to gasoline to prevent knocking, phased out starting in the 1970s with catalytic converters.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Hosts take a break between segments.

segments.title: Lead in the earth, smelting and recycling
segments.summary: Lead occurs in compounds such as oxides and sulfides, often with silver. Ancient Roman cupellation is described, along with modern roasting and smelting of galena, slag and pig lead, and secondary extraction from car batteries.

segments.title: Lead health effects and blood testing
segments.summary: The body treats lead like calcium, disrupting neurons and brain development in children and affecting many organ systems. Blood lead thresholds, home test kits and the zinc protoporphyrin test are discussed. Treatments include succimer and chelation therapy, along with nutrition.

segments.title: Lead and crime hypothesis
segments.summary: Discussion of the Mother Jones article by Kevin Drum linking childhood lead exposure from leaded gasoline to later crime rates, plus scientific skepticism from Scott Firestone and the call for cohort studies.

segments.title: Flint lawsuits and liability
segments.summary: Lawsuits over Flint water, obstacles such as sovereign immunity and proving specific causation, the corrosion control failure, and a suggested victim compensation fund modeled on Deepwater Horizon.

segments.title: Listener mail: Finland and low corruption
segments.summary: Listener Gabrielle, an American living in Helsinki, writes about low political corruption, the multiparty system and high taxes in Finland.
